tier_reason: The goja comparison meets A. The runners are public (internal/cmd/v8bench/main.go, internal/cmd/v8bench/goja/main.go, internal/v8bench/v8bench.go), the exact commands and revisions are pinned (go-quickjs 04bbeec, goja 793a2a6, AreWeFastYet 0e21608), it was built with Go 1.27.0 using default `go run` flags, and it ran on an Apple M5 Max. The C QuickJS comparison (internal/cmd/v8bench/external, Ryzen 5 3600, Go 1.27.1) does not state how the qjs binary was built, so on its own that half would be C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 with default `go run` build flags for the goja comparison (go-quickjs 04bbeec, goja 793a2a6, AreWeFastYet v8-v7 0e21608; commands `go run ./internal/cmd/v8bench -dir /tmp/v8-v7 -mode score` and the goja runner in internal/cmd/v8bench/goja). Go 1.27.1 for the C QuickJS comparison (go-quickjs 4629679 / v0.21.1, `-mode fixed -n 3` plus score mode, with QuickJS run via internal/cmd/v8bench/external `-engine qjs`). The page does not say how the C QuickJS 2026-06-04 binary was built (compiler, flags, or official Windows build).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from a very young project (3 stars, 0 forks). Against C QuickJS the result is mixed. In the suite's own scores go-quickjs trails QuickJS on 5 of 8 workloads (Richards 692 vs 941, DeltaBlue 764 vs 840, EarleyBoyer 2,033 vs 2,162, Splay 2,968 vs 3,297, NavierStokes 2,302 vs 2,420). The 11% higher composite comes mostly from RegExp (1,409 vs 390, 3.61x; derived from page data). In fixed-run time it loses Richards, DeltaBlue, EarleyBoyer and NavierStokes, and its 0.65x total comes from RegExp (0.30x) and Splay's allocation-heavy setup. Single operations are slower: 1.15x QuickJS's time by geometric mean over 71 tests of QuickJS's microbench.js, slower on 48, up to 3.5x on weak_map_set. The author says figures move by a few percent between builds from code placement alone, and Richards and DeltaBlue by up to a tenth. The goja and QuickJS comparisons ran on different machines and operating systems (Apple M5 Max vs Ryzen 5 3600 on Windows), and the qjs build is unstated. No V8/Node numbers are published, although the runner supports `-engine node`, so the category incumbent V8 is not measured; the baselines actually tested (QuickJS, goja) are embedded-scripting incumbents. It is a pure-Go reimplementation of QuickJS-NG, and the MIT LICENSE carries the QuickJS/QuickJS-NG copyrights (Bellard, Gordon, Noordhuis, Ibarra Corretge). The search agent found it through the go-js-engines-benchmark shootout snippet (written by the author of the competing QJS engine).

notes: All claimed numbers match docs/benchmarks.md exactly: goja composite 3,748 vs 720 (5.21x), wall time 22.51 s vs 53.37 s, 60.2% less allocation; QuickJS 1,690 ms vs 2,589 ms (0.65x), composite 1,454 vs 1,315; micro-benchmark geomean 1.15x, 48 of 71 slower. The A tier rests on the goja comparison; the headline win over C QuickJS is RegExp-driven and loses 5 of 8 workloads by score, so record that as a shortcoming. Possible duplicate question: this is a Go reimplementation of QuickJS-NG, and bellard/quickjs and goja are already listed (embedded-scripting). It is an independent engine with its own measured profile, so I did not reject it as known-project; the orchestrator decides under the port precedent (m77rip, miara).

tier_reason: manuals/benchmarks.md gives the exact commands, clang 9.0.1 and three flag sets used for both bcs (-O2; -O3 -flto -march=native; -O3 -flto), best of four runs, but no CPU model ('x86_64 machine running Gentoo Linux'). The scripts it uses (tests/bc/add.bc etc.) belong to the bc 3.0.0 tree and are no longer at those paths, so this is first-party evidence with partial methodology: C.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 253 stars, 42 forks, 6,072 commits; per the README it is the system bc in FreeBSD, macOS and Android (AOSP external/bc) and in several Linux distributions, and it is packaged in Fedora
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from bc 3.0.0 (2019) against GNU bc 1.07.1, built with clang 9.0.1 on an unnamed x86_64 CPU, best of four runs. The project has had many releases since, and the benchmark scripts' paths (tests/bc/add.bc) no longer exist in the current tree. The wall-clock gains on add/subtract/multiply/divide are inflated by 1.3-2.5 s of sys time in GNU bc's runs (cause not stated on the page). By user time the -O2 gains are 1.42x add, 1.24x subtract, 2.23x multiply, 1.19x divide and 1.22x timeconst.bc, against 2.89x, 2.76x, 3.25x, 2.09x and 1.27x by wall time (all derived from page data). The power test (1234567890^100000) is the clear win at 15.7x user time. The interpreter itself is not faster: at -O2 the 100,000,000-iteration for-loop script is slower (22.76 s vs 16.60 s) and the while-loop script is level (16.98 s vs 17.32 s). The author also found -march=native makes this bc slower. GNU bc is not one of the category baselines (CPython, Lua, Ruby, V8), and bc is a calculator language rather than a general scripting language. The author calls bc complete (no new features) but still actively maintained.

notes: All claimed numbers appear in manuals/benchmarks.md, attributed correctly (-O2: add 2.54 vs 0.88 s, mult 7.15 vs 2.20, div 3.36 vs 1.61, power 11.30 vs 0.73, timeconst 16.71 vs 13.16; -O3 -flto -march=native: power 11.08 vs 0.71, mult 7.01 vs 1.59; for-loop 16.60 GNU vs 22.76 this bc). Shortcomings to record: off-baseline (GNU bc), no CPU model, 2019 version, and arithmetic wins partly sys-time driven. It is notable as the system bc of FreeBSD, macOS and Android. BSD-2-Clause, last commit 2026-10-03.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. docs/benchmarks.adoc is the generated output of the public nix derivation nix/benchmarks.nix at commit 4824700 (hyperfine -N -w4 -m20, with the 'takes longer than a hour' note and table format matching). The toolchains are pinned by flake.lock (nixpkgs a124a10ea33a and rust-overlay 9922ff9f99a6, both 2026-02-07; rustc from rust-toolchain.toml channel stable). Flags are public: jrsonnet's Cargo [profile.release] (opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, mimalloc), and C++ jsonnet rev d33798d built with its Makefile (g++, OPT ?= -O3). The CPU is stated (Ryzen 9 9950X3D). Compiler version numbers are not printed, only pinned; if the orchestrator requires named versions, this falls back to C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Built and run by the repo's nix flake at doc commit 4824700 (docs/benchmarks.adoc 'chore: re-run benchmarks', 2026-04-01). Toolchains pinned by flake.lock: nixpkgs a124a10ea33a and rust-overlay 9922ff9f99a6 (both 2026-02-07); rustc comes from rust-toolchain.toml (channel stable) via rust-overlay. jrsonnet 0.5.0-pre97 uses Cargo [profile.release] opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, --features=mimalloc. C++ jsonnet (google/jsonnet rev d33798d, reported as v0.22.0-rc1) is built with its Makefile `make jsonnet` (CXX g++, OPT ?= -O3) under nix stdenv. Both are wrapped with --max-stack 200000. Driver: hyperfine -N -w4 -m20 (nix/benchmarks.nix). Compiler version numbers are not printed in the doc.
corrections.caveats: This is the maintainer's own benchmark. It is reproducible through the pinned nix flake (nix/benchmarks.nix), but the hyperfine driver never compares outputs between implementations. Rows in microseconds (Tail call, Inheritance function recursion, String strips, Big object, manifestJsonEx, manifestTomlEx, parseInt, substr) sit at a ~750-900 us floor for jrsonnet and are dominated by process startup. C++ jsonnet was not run on the heaviest workloads (GraalVM CI, kube-prometheus, Large string template, Realistic 1/2, String strips, base64, Comparison for array/primitives) because it took hours. Where C++ did run, jrsonnet is faster on every row, by a smallest margin of 1.89x on Lazy array and 2.20x on Simple recursive call (derived from page data). Several >50x rows (Array sorts 1,531x, base64Decode 4,069x, Inheritance function recursion 1,061x) reflect C++ jsonnet's algorithmic slowness rather than a like-for-like engine. jrsonnet is not the fastest on every row: Scala native wins Inheritance recursion, Simple recursive call and Comparison for primitives, rsjsonnet wins Lazy array, and Scala GraalVM wins std.base64 (byte array). The C++ and Go baselines are release candidates (v0.22.0-rc1). The repo was renamed from CertainLach/jrsonnet, which redirects to deltarocks/jrsonnet.

notes: All claimed numbers match docs/benchmarks.adoc: Large string join 2.6 ms vs C++ 39.7 (15.44x) vs Go 46.4; Tail call 865.2 us vs C++ 18,460.1 us (21.34x) vs Go 2,559.0 us (2.96x); GraalVM CI 34.4 ms vs Go 600.3 (17.47x); kube-prometheus 43.6 vs Go 1,068.4 (24.52x). The upgrade to A rests on the pinned public nix harness. Shortcomings to record: outputs are not compared, the microsecond rows are startup-dominated, C++ is omitted on the heavy workloads, and Scala native beats jrsonnet on 3 rows. The same doc already raised databricks/sjsonnet to B, so the two records should stay consistent. MIT, last commit 2026-08-31, 374 stars.
